newsitem.title: ITALY: Grenade found in Florence amid Italian alert.
newsitem.headline: Grenade found in Florence amid Italian alert.

text.p: Police found an unexploded World War Two hand grenade near the Ponte Vecchio bridge in Florence on Friday as Italy went on alert following an intelligence report that Islamic extremists may be planning attacks.

The grenade, spotted in the courtyard of a building by the River Arno by a local resident, was removed by bomb disposal experts and blown up in a controlled explosion, police in the Tuscan city said by telephone.
Florence police chief Francesco Forleo told reporters that the aged grenade may have been planted as a "act of intimidation" by someone trying to cause a scare.
He said it would be "illogical" to link the incident to the extremism report. The find led lunchtime television news bulletins after security forces went on alert across Italy.

The alert was prompted by a military intelligence report, leaked to the national news agency ANSA on Thursday, that Islamic extremists may be preparing to attack targets in Italy including Pope John Paul and international airports.

Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Angelo Sodano told Italian television that the Pope, who was seriously injured by a Turkish gunman in 1981, was not "particularly alarmed" by the purported threats.
The 76-year-old Pontiff's spokesman, Joaquin Navarro-Valls, declined to say whether any special precautions had been taken.
"For obvious reasons, we do not comment on reports that concern matters of security," Navarro-Valls said in a statement.

Security measures were increased at airports in Milan and Rome, with police at the capital's Fiumicino airport using explosives experts and sniffer dogs to check planes of European, U.S. and Middle Eastern carriers, security sources said.

ANSA said the report sounding the alarm had been drawn up by the Italian military intelligence agency SISMI and referred to the crisis in Europe's relations with Iran as the possible spark for attacks by Islamic militants.
The Interior Ministry declined to comment but a leading Italian anti-terrorism investigator, prosecuting magistrate Rosario Priore, said there was some foundation to the threat.
"I don't think it is totally unfounded. There are many signs (including) above all a chain of attacks against religious targets," Priore told Italian radio.
"In my opinion this means we should not overlook or exclude the possibility of Islamic extremism," he said.
Priore is leading continuing investigations into the 1981 shooting of the Pope in St Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Agca, now serving a life sentence in an Italian jail.
The Pope's visit last weekend to the predominantly Moslem Bosnian capital Sarajevo was preceded by the discovery of land mines planted along the route of his motorcade.

The Roman Catholic leader continued with his Sarajevo visit despite the discovery of the 23 land mines, planted under a road bridge into Sarajevo from the airport. The mines, attached to a detonator, were defused a few hours before he arrived.

Priore is conducting inquiries into whether members of the Turkish right-wing Grey Wolves group may have had a role in the 1981 papal assassination attempt and has asked Bosnian authorities for a report on last weekend's scare.
